newsitem.title: USA: Republicans ram through funds for campaign probe.
newsitem.headline: Republicans ram through funds for campaign probe.

text.p: Over the objections of Democrats, Republicans drove approval of $4.35 million through a key committee Thursday to start an investigation of illegal campaign activities in the 1996 elections.

The plan, hammered out by Senate Republican majority leader Trent Lott to get the stalled investigation going, was approved by the Senate Rules Committee on a vote of nine Republicans to six Democrats, and will go to the Republican-controlled Senate for approval next week.

It was the most definitive congressional action to date to get the investigation under way. A House committee also is seeking money for its separate probe to focus on questionable activities involving President Clinton's re-election.

The funding plan approved for the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee probe to be headed by Tennessee Republican Sen. Fred Thompson would limit the investigation to "illegal" activities of Clinton's campaign, his opponent Bob Dole's campaign and congressional races.

But Democrats led by Ohio Democratic Sen. John Glenn charged that narrowing the scope to "illegal" activities would bar the committee from investigating improper or unethical dealings, especially in politically sensitive congressional races or unregulated 'soft money' donations.

Thompson's committee had recently approved a broad scope which would have given it sweeping powers to investigate, but Republican leaders turned that plan down during private meetings for a more restrictive probe.
Thompson reluctantly agreed to the narrower investigation to keep his committee probe alive.

Before it approved the Republican plan, devised by Lott and Rules Committee chairman John Warner, a Virginia Republican, the committee rejected in a party-line vote a Democratic substitute plan to expand the scope.
Sen. Christopher Dodd, a Connecticut Democrat who was chairman of the party under fire for accepting illegal and questionable donations to help Clinton, abstained.

The Rules committee vote capped a day of clashes in Congress by Republicans and Democrats over funding. At issue was how much money the Republican-controlled Congress would approve for the probes and whether they would include congressional campaign wrongdoing.

The campaign finance uproar has been a major embarrassment during Clinton's second term as reports emerged over questionable funds. Besides pending congressional probes, an FBI task force is investigating illegalities.

Thompson originally wanted $6.5 million, then $5.7 million. Democrats led by Glenn had demanded the investigation cover congressional races as well as improprieties in the presidential election, a limit to the duration of hearings and a set date for discussing campaign finance reform.

In an effort to compromise, Lott proposed giving the committee $4.35 million, stipulating the investigation stop at the end of the year and expanding its scope to cover all allegedly "illegal" activities in federal campaigns, the plan later approved by the rules group.

On the House side, the chief investigator, House Government Reform committee chairman Dan Burton, an Indiana Republican, asked the House Oversight Committee for $3.8 million to investigate "alleged fund-raising abuses of the Clinton administration and the Democratic National Committee."

Representative Henry Waxman, a California Democrat who is senior minority member on Burton's committee, charged that Burton was running a "one-sided" investigation that would exclude congressional fund raising. He also said Democrats were not getting enough money out of Burton's committee request.
